cards.title: Show HN: dp_intl – Gettext-compatible internationalization library for C++

signals.title: Show HN: dp_intl – Gettext-compatible internationalization library for C++
signals.description:
dp_intl is intended to be an enhanced version of the Gettext runtime library (also known as libintl), with the following improvements:

* dp_intl does not depend on the locale. In contrast, Gettext requires the use of the setlocale() function from the C standard library, which alters the behavior of other locale-dependent C routines, leading to subtle bugs that only arise in specific locales. For example, a floating-point number serialized by snprintf() with a locale that uses a period as a decimal separator will not be parsed correctly by strtof() with a locale that uses a comma, and vice versa. Another example is tolower() and strcasecmp(), which will break with the Turkish locale, where the lowercase of "I" is "ı" rather than "i".

* dp_intl uses 64-bit integers for plural form routines on all platforms. In contrast, Gettext routines (e.g. ngettext()) use the unsigned long type, making it impossible to write cross-platform code without limiting your numbers to 2³² (4,294,967,295). Otherwise, translations for numbers greater than 2³² will have incorrect plural forms due to unsigned wrap around (modulo 2³²) on systems with a 32-bit unsigned long (e.g., 64-bit Windows).

* Unlike Gettext, dp_intl is not tied to local file system: it reads files through a virtual stream class that can wrap any file-like object, including those from archives and packages (like an APK on Android).

* dp_intl allows any language in source strings. In contrast, the Gettext routines for translating plural form messages (e.g., ngettext()) are limited to English and several other languages with two plural forms: "one" for 1 and "many" for all other numbers, making it impossible to use any other language that doesn't fit this pattern.

CsvPath Framework is a Python data firewall that protects downstream systems from bad data getting past the ingress point. Data is much easier to fix when you shift quality control left, remove manual data checking, stop accumulating orphaned ingestion code, and decrease the skills consumed by data pipelines.

The Framework:

- registers inbound data into an immutable, versioned staging area, with a cryptographic identity,

- validates and upgrades it using one or more of five validation languages,

- generates ops and lineage metadata for OpenLineage and OpenTelemetry,

- and publishes results data and metadata to a versioned immutable archive with no-code integrations downstream.

CsvPath Framework refers to these bullets as "data preboarding".

cards.title: Show HN: Real Design Benchmark – can you tell AI designs from real products?

signals.title: Show HN: Real Design Benchmark – can you tell AI designs from real products?
signals.description:
Hi HN,

I'm Adam Ginzberg, one of the cofounders of Subframe, a code-first design tool.

One of the things I'm really curious about is understanding LLM performance on subjective domains like design.

As an experiment I built this game which presents two designs of the same screen, one of which was generated by AI. First you pick which one you like better and then which one you think was made by AI.

Most design work happens in an existing product, so we set up this game to test that. As context, the AI gets 4 screenshots from the existing product, the product's icons + fonts, and a written brief about the screen it is asked to build. It then writes HTML which is screenshotted identically to the real screen. To get the data, we signed up for the products with test accounts and added dummy data. All of the inputs were manually checked to make sure nothing about the target screen was leaked in the prompt. You can read more about the methodology at https://www.realdesignbenchmark.com/methodology.

After a few thousand submissions, the surprising result is that people prefer the AI design - 57% prefer AI, 33% prefer the real design, 10% say they are about the same. People are also not great at identifying the AI design, only 59% get it right.

The initial results were all generated with Opus 5.5 (medium effort). We just added GPT-6.1 Sol (medium effort) tonight.

Give the game a try. Feedback on the approach is appreciated. Or any ideas on what we might improve or try next.

cards.title: Show HN: Parsimony – an open-source benchmark for how much code AI models add

signals.title: Show HN: Parsimony – an open-source benchmark for how much code AI models add
signals.description:
Existing benchmarks measure solve rate and token output/cost, but don't punish excess code, which makes a codebase harder to work with in the long term. I wanted to measure this since it matters most for long-term projects.

Method: it takes the patches that benchmarks already publish (DeepSWE, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Live) and counts "coding units": syntax elements like statements, calls, names and literals. I didn't use lines of code, so cramming code isn't rewarded. Deleted code is subtracted, so it measures net units.

GPT-6 and Claude 5.5 have no public patches yet, so I ran them myself on 3–10 tasks on my own subscriptions (shown as faded circles, not ranked).

Any feedback or model contributions are welcome, especially public patch exports for newer models.

GitHub: https://github.com/La5u/Parsimony

Not affiliated with any of the benchmarks.
